title: What training do hospice aides need under 42 CFR 418.76?
description: Hospice aide rules in 42 CFR 418.76 and hospice staff training in 418.100(g): training hours, competency, in-service and 14-day RN visits, at November 2026.
shortAnswer: Under 42 CFR 418.76, a hospice aide must complete at least 75 hours of combined classroom and supervised practical training and a registered nurse's competency evaluation, or qualify through a competency evaluation alone, a state nurse aide program with registry standing, or state licensure. Each aide then needs at least 12 hours of in-service training every 12 months. A registered nurse must visit the patient's home at least every 14 days to supervise aide care.
keyTakeaways: The aide standard sits in the hospice Conditions of Participation at 42 CFR 418.76, while orientation and competence duties for all hospice staff sit in 418.100(g).
Training content has 13 subject areas, from communication and vital signs to a personal hygiene checklist and nutrition, plus any other task the hospice assigns.
A registered nurse must make an on-site supervisory visit at least every 14 days and observe each aide providing care at least once a year.
If the supervising nurse verifies a concern on site, the aide must complete a competency evaluation of the deficient skill and all related skills.
Every employee with patient and family contact must be oriented to the hospice philosophy, and the hospice must keep a written description of in-service training from the previous 12 months.
regulator: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), US Department of Health and Human Services
appliesTo: Hospices participating in Medicare and Medicaid
Hospice aides and homemakers, whether employed or furnished under arrangement
All hospice employees and contracted staff with patient and family contact (418.100(g)), and volunteers (418.78)

sections.heading: How does a hospice aide qualify under 418.76?

blocks.text: A hospice aide qualifies by completing one of four programs listed in [42 CFR 418.76(a)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-B/part-418/subpart-C/section-418.76): the hospice's training program followed by a competency evaluation; a competency evaluation program alone; a state-approved nurse aide training and competency evaluation program with current good standing on the state nurse aide registry; or a state licensure program.

The qualification expires through non-use. A continuous 24-month period in which the person furnished no compensated aide services means they must complete another qualifying program before working again. The state licensure route in hospice is worded more briefly than in the home health rule, which also requires the licensure program to meet the training and competency standards; hospices relying on that route should confirm what the state program covers. This page states the position as at November 2026, based on eCFR text current to November 5, 2026.

sections.heading: What must hospice aide training include?

blocks.text: Classroom and supervised practical training combined must total at least 75 hours, with at least 16 hours of classroom training completed before at least 16 hours of supervised practical training. Practical training happens in a practicum laboratory or other setting where the trainee performs tasks on an individual under direct supervision of a registered nurse, or a licensed practical nurse working under a registered nurse.

blocks.text: The home health aide rule lists one subject that 418.76 does not: recognizing and reporting changes in skin condition. A hospice can still add it under item (xiii) where aides are expected to report skin changes. Instructors must be registered nurses with at least 2 years of nursing experience, at least 1 year of which is in home care, or other individuals under a registered nurse's general supervision. For the home health version, see [home health aide training requirements](/regulations/home-health-aide-training-requirements).

sections.heading: What happens in the hospice aide competency evaluation?

blocks.text: An individual may furnish hospice aide services only after passing a competency evaluation that addresses every subject in 418.76(b)(3), performed by a registered nurse in consultation with other skilled professionals as appropriate. The five hands-on subjects must be observed with a patient or pseudo-patient, as shown in the table above.

A task rated unsatisfactory may not be performed without direct supervision by a registered nurse until the aide has been retrained and passes a later evaluation. More than one unsatisfactory area means the evaluation has not been passed. Competency evaluation programs may be offered by any organization except a home health agency that, in the previous 2 years, was out of compliance with the home health aide rules or was subject to the sanctions listed in 418.76(f), such as a civil monetary penalty of $5,000 or more.

sections.heading: What in-service training and supervision continue after hire?

blocks.text: Every hospice aide must receive at least 12 hours of in-service training during each 12-month period, which may take place while the aide is caring for a patient and must be supervised by a registered nurse. Supervision is more uniform in hospice than in home health: under 418.76(h), a registered nurse must make an on-site visit to the patient's home no less frequently than every 14 days to assess the aide's services, and the aide need not be present.

blocks.title: 42 CFR 418.76(h)(1)(iii): verified concerns
blocks.text: "If an area of concern is verified by the hospice during the on-site visit, then the hospice must conduct, and the hospice aide must complete, a competency evaluation of the deficient skill and all related skill(s) in accordance with paragraph (c) of this section."

Separately, a registered nurse must make an annual on-site visit to observe and assess each aide while performing care. The supervising nurse assesses outcome criteria that include following the plan of care, building successful relationships with the patient and family, demonstrating competency with assigned tasks, complying with infection control policies, and reporting changes in the patient's condition. These criteria can double as the observation checklist for the annual visit.

sections.heading: What orientation and competence duties apply to all hospice staff?

blocks.text: Beyond aides, [42 CFR 418.100(g)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-B/part-418/subpart-D/section-418.100) requires a hospice to orient all employees and contracted staff who have patient and family contact to the hospice philosophy, and to give each employee an initial orientation on their specific job duties. The hospice must also assess the skills and competence of everyone furnishing care, including volunteers, and provide in-service training where needed.

Two documents are required under 418.100(g)(3): written policies and procedures describing how the hospice assesses competency, and a written description of the in-service training provided during the previous 12 months. Homemakers must complete hospice orientation on the needs of patients and families coping with terminal illness (418.76(j)), and volunteers must receive orientation and training consistent with hospice industry standards (418.78(a)). Hospice staff must also make sure facility staff caring for hospice patients in a nursing facility are oriented to hospice policies (418.112(f)). Emergency preparedness training is due at hire and at least every 2 years under [42 CFR 418.113(d)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-B/part-418/subpart-D/section-418.113).

blocks.text: Organizing by role makes the overlapping duties manageable. The register below is illustrative and should be extended for clinical disciplines and any state requirements.

blocks.text: A [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) with these rows lets the hospice show any surveyor the status of each person at a glance, and [role-based training](/glossary/role-based-training) keeps homemakers and volunteers from being assigned the full aide curriculum.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links the 418.76 subject areas, the supervising nurse's outcome criteria and the hospice's own competency policy into one structure, so an area of concern found on a visit points to the specific skill and its related skills for reevaluation. See how this works for [healthcare and life sciences organizations](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences).

faqs.q: Can a home health aide work as a hospice aide?
faqs.a: Often, if the person meets one of the 418.76(a) routes, such as a state-approved nurse aide program with good registry standing or a competency evaluation that meets 418.76(c). The hospice must verify qualification and keep documentation. The 24-month lapse rule applies, and the hospice must still supervise and provide in-service training.

faqs.q: Can the 14-day supervisory visit be done by video?
faqs.a: The current hospice rule at 418.76(h)(1)(i) calls for an on-site visit to the patient's home no less frequently than every 14 days. Unlike the home health aide rule, the hospice text read for this page does not include a limited virtual supervision option, so hospices should plan for in-person visits.

faqs.q: Does a hospice have to keep in-service training records?
faqs.a: Yes. 418.76(d)(2) requires documentation that aide in-service requirements are met, and 418.100(g)(3) requires a written description of the in-service training provided during the previous 12 months, along with written policies describing how the hospice assesses competency.

Yes. 42 CFR 418.78(a) requires the hospice to maintain, document and provide volunteer orientation and training consistent with hospice industry standards. Volunteers who furnish care are also within the 418.100(g)(3) duty to assess skills and competence.

factCheck.claim: 418.76(a): four routes including state licensure program (no cross-reference to (b) and (c)); 24 consecutive months without compensated services requires new program. eCFR current to 2026-11-05; last amended 86 FR 42605, Aug. 4, 2021.

418.76(b): at least 75 hours combined; 16 classroom hours precede 16 supervised practical hours; 13 subject areas (no separate skin condition item); (e) instructors RN with 2 years experience, 1 year in home care.
418.76(c): evaluation before service; (b)(3)(i), (iii), (ix), (x), (xi) observed; RN performs; unsatisfactory rules; (f) HHA exclusions incl. CMP of $5,000 or more within previous 2 years.

418.76(d): at least 12 hours in-service per 12-month period, RN supervised; (h)(1) RN on-site visit at least every 14 days; (h)(1)(iii) competency evaluation of deficient and related skills; (h)(2) annual on-site observation; (h)(3) outcome criteria; (j) homemaker orientation.

418.100(g)(1)-(3): hospice philosophy orientation for employees and contracted staff with patient and family contact; job-specific orientation; assess skills and competence including volunteers; written competency policies; written description of in-service training in previous 12 months.
418.78(a): volunteer orientation and training consistent with hospice industry standards. 418.112(f): orientation of SNF/NF or ICF/IID staff (read in full part 418 text).

418.113(d)(1): initial emergency preparedness training for new and existing employees and those under arrangement; demonstrate knowledge; at least every 2 years; documentation; training after significant updates.
